questions.prompt: An ultrasonic sensor's echo pin stays HIGH for 5 ms. Using a speed of sound of 343 m/s, how far away is the object, in centimeters? Round to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: distance = (343 × 0.005) / 2 = 0.8575 m = 85.75 cm; the pulse travels there and back, so divide by 2.

questions.prompt: An NTC thermistor's resistance decreases as its temperature rises.
questions.explanation: NTC means negative temperature coefficient: resistance falls as temperature rises.

questions.prompt: Why is a normally closed (NC) limit switch often preferred for safety-critical limits such as an emergency stop?
choices: A broken wire looks the same as a triggered switch, so a fault fails into the stop state
It draws no current at all
It produces an analog voltage proportional to force
It never needs a pull-up resistor
questions.answer: A broken wire looks the same as a triggered switch, so a fault fails into the stop state
questions.explanation: With an NC switch a disconnected wire opens the circuit, just like a press, so the fault is treated as a stop.

questions.prompt: A stepper motor moves 1.8° per step. How many steps are needed to rotate the shaft 90°?
questions.explanation: 90 / 1.8 = 50 steps (200 steps make a full 360° turn).

questions.prompt: Match each component to its key characteristic.
pairs: Spins continuously but has no built-in position awareness
Built-in position feedback holds a commanded angle
Moves in fixed steps and can silently miss steps under stall
Lets a motor be driven in either direction from low-power control signals
questions.explanation: Each pairing comes from the actuator and driver descriptions in this unit.

questions.prompt: Which actuator tracks its position only by counting commanded steps and therefore cannot detect a stall on its own?
choices: Stepper motor
Servo motor
Plain DC motor with an encoder
H-bridge
questions.explanation: A stepper has no feedback sensor, so a stall can make the real position differ from the step count without the controller noticing.

questions.prompt: A 5 V GPIO pin drives a red LED (about 2 V forward drop) through a 220 Ω resistor. What current flows, in milliamps? Round to two decimal places.
Which of these keep their contents when power is removed?
choices: Flash memory
EEPROM
RAM
A running program's variables held in RAM
questions.explanation: Flash and EEPROM are non-volatile; RAM is volatile and loses everything without power.

questions.prompt: In a microcontroller program, pin configuration normally goes in the one-time setup phase, while sensing and reacting belongs in the repeating loop phase.
questions.explanation: Configuration only needs to happen once; sensing and acting must repeat for as long as power is on.

questions.prompt: A 12-bit ADC uses a 5 V reference. What is its step size in millivolts? Round to two decimal places.
What is the trade-off of increasing the window size of a moving average filter?
choices: Smoother output but more lag behind real changes
Faster response but more noise
Higher ADC resolution
More PWM duty cycle range
questions.answer: Smoother output but more lag behind real changes
questions.explanation: A longer window averages more readings, suppressing noise but letting old readings linger.

questions.prompt: What is the small, unavoidable rounding error introduced when an ADC maps a continuous voltage to a discrete level called? (two words)
questions.explanation: Quantization error is the difference between the true voltage and the nearest reported level, at most half a step.

questions.prompt: A microwave that runs for a fixed 90 seconds without measuring food temperature is an example of open-loop control.
questions.explanation: Open-loop control follows a predetermined plan with no sensor checking the actual result.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of one pass through a closed-loop (feedback) controller in order, starting with the sensor reading.
items: Measure the actual output with a sensor
Compute the error as setpoint minus measured value
Convert the error into an actuator command
The actuator changes the system, which changes the output
questions.explanation: Feedback measures first, forms the error, commands a correction, and the result is measured again next pass.

questions.prompt: Explain what chattering is in a bang-bang controller and how adding hysteresis (a deadband) fixes it.
rubric: Says a single threshold plus sensor noise causes rapid on/off switching at the setpoint
Says hysteresis uses two thresholds, one to turn on and a different one to turn off
Says the actuator stays in its state until the opposite threshold is crossed
Mentions the trade-off of a looser hold on the setpoint
questions.model: With one threshold, noise near the setpoint makes the reading cross it repeatedly, so the actuator switches on and off rapidly. Hysteresis uses a lower threshold to switch on and a higher one to switch off, so the actuator holds its state until the opposite threshold is crossed. The cost is that the value oscillates within the wider band rather than sitting near the setpoint.
questions.explanation: Two thresholds stop noise from toggling the actuator, at the cost of looser control.

questions.prompt: A PID controller has Kp = 3, Ki = 0.2, Kd = 2. At one instant the error is 5, the accumulated integral of error is 20, and the rate of change of error is −2. What is the controller output (before clamping)?
Which statements about PID terms are correct?
choices: The integral term eliminates steady-state error left by pure P control
The derivative term damps the approach to the setpoint and reduces overshoot
A derivative term can amplify sensor noise
The proportional term alone always drives the error exactly to zero
answers: The integral term eliminates steady-state error left by pure P control
The derivative term damps the approach to the setpoint and reduces overshoot
A derivative term can amplify sensor noise
questions.explanation: Pure P control often settles with a small offset, which the I term removes; D anticipates changes but is sensitive to noise.

questions.prompt: What is the name for the problem where the integral term keeps accumulating while the actuator is saturated?
questions.explanation: Integral windup is when accumulated error grows far beyond what the actuator can act on, causing large overshoot afterward.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the subsystem design recipe in order.
items: Pick a sensor for the quantity to control
Pick an actuator that can affect that quantity
Choose a control strategy matched to the actuator
Add filtering if the sensor is noisy
Write the setup/loop program tying read, decide, and write together
questions.explanation: The recipe goes from sensing to actuation to control strategy, then filtering, then the program.

questions.prompt: In a program that has a safety condition (such as an over-temperature check) alongside normal control, how should the safety condition be handled?
choices: Check it first and let it override the normal control output entirely
Average it into the control calculation with the other inputs
Run it only after the control loop finishes
Ignore it unless the actuator is a relay
questions.answer: Check it first and let it override the normal control output entirely
questions.explanation: A safety condition should bypass the normal control math, not be blended in as one more input.

questions.prompt: Describe how you should debug an integrated sensor + control + actuator system that is not working, and why.
rubric: Says to test the sensor alone first and check its values make sense
Says to test the actuator alone with a fixed output value
Says to combine them only after each works independently
Gives a symptom to cause example such as noisy output pointing to missing filtering or persistent oscillation pointing to tuning
questions.model: Test the sensor by itself and confirm its readings make physical sense, then drive the actuator alone with a fixed value to confirm it responds. Only then connect them in the closed loop. This isolates where a fault is; for example, erratic output suggests unfiltered noise and persistent oscillation suggests gains that are too aggressive.
questions.explanation: Isolating each piece first makes it clear which part is responsible for a failure.

questions.prompt: Match each real-world system to its control feature.
pairs: Rapid on/off pulsing of brake pressure (bang-bang style)
Separate PID loops for roll, pitch, and yaw using an IMU
Ruggedized industrial controller programmed in ladder logic
Encoder feedback into a per-joint control loop
questions.explanation: Each system applies the sensor, controller, actuator pattern in its own way.

questions.prompt: A PLC runs the same basic read-decide-write cycle as a microcontroller, but is ruggedized for factory environments and traditionally programmed in ladder logic.
questions.explanation: PLCs solve the same loop problem with a different notation and tougher hardware built for reliability.

questions.prompt: Which sensor combination does a drone use to measure its tilt and rotation rate for stabilization?
choices: An IMU containing an accelerometer and a gyroscope
A limit switch and a thermistor
An ultrasonic sensor and a photoresistor
A thermocouple and an encoder
questions.answer: An IMU containing an accelerometer and a gyroscope
questions.explanation: The inertial measurement unit supplies the tilt and rotation data the stabilization loops need.
